newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WTO body confirms meat hormone ruling against EU.
newsitem.headline: WTO body confirms meat hormone ruling against EU.

text.p: A World Trade Organisation (WTO) dispute panel has confirmed a initial finding that a European Union ban on imports of hormone-treated meat violates open trading rules, trade sources said on Tuesday.

The final ruling, coming down in favour of a complaint by the United States, was delivered to EU and U.S. missions in Geneva on Monday and the two governments were expected to reveal its contents formally later on Tuesday.

Washington had been backed in its complaint by Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Norway. Argentina, which exports beef untreated with hormones to many EU member states, voiced support for the Brussels position.
Trade diplomats said the EU was certain to appeal the finding, which would postpone for several more months any need for Brussels to take action to lift the 11-year-old ban.

EU officials have indicated they see little prospect of lifting the restrictions, which were officially imposed for health reasons, because of strong consumer pressure against sale of beef treated with hormones.

If Brussels loses an appeal -- as is almost certain -- but still declines to act, the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) could request the EU to pay compensation to the United States for the amount of trade it says it has lost.
If the EU were to refuse, the DSB -- on which all the WTO's currently 131 members have a voice -- could authorise U.S. trade retaliation to the same amount.

In 1989, two years after first bringing the case to the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), the United States slapped 10 per cent duties on a range of agricultural goods from the EU worth around $90 million a year.

In July last year, the EU asked the DSB to set up a panel to look into the legality of the U.S. counter-action, but two weeks later Washington announced it was lifting the duties pending a decision in its case against Brussels.
When the initial ruling by the three-man panel was sent to Brussels and Washington in May, the United States hailed the finding as backing its argument that the EU ban had no scientific basis.
U.S. Agriculture Department officials said at the time they wanted to see the EU market opened and were not especially interested in compensation.
According to the U.S. beef industry, the ban has reduced sales to EU countries by at least $100 million a year and as much as $250 million annually.
